newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma slams govt for agricultural reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma slams govt for agricultural reforms.

text.p: Russia's State Duma lower parliament house approved on Friday a resolution condemning the government's market-style reforms in the farm sector and slammed a well-known regional pilot project as inapplicable.
The non-binding resolution, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, called for the government to declare its agricultural reforms a mistake and reverse them, but did not outline alternatives.
In voting on the measure, 257 deputies supported the document, four deputies voted against it and three abstained.

"The Nizhny Novogorod model suggested by the Russian government as a model for reforming agricultural organisations is not effective," the resolution said, referring to the most famous farm-reform project in the country.

Nizhny Novgorod is home to a voluntary privatisation project spearheaded by the International Finance Corporation, the private sector arm of the World Bank. But the experiment has failed so far to take root across the rest of the country.
Russia's flagging agriculture sector has seen some changes, but it is in the throes of a deep crisis in which output has plunged and former collective farms, now privatised, are nearly bankrupt.
The collapse has meant imports now fill 50 percent of the domestic food market, threatening Russia's ability to feed itself and independence from foreign supplies, the resolution said.
It said 70 percent of farms were insolvent, livestock numbers had plunged 50 percent, sheep numbers 80 percent and 18 million hectares of arable farmland were no longer in use.
Grain yields had halved as fertiliser use declined, while farming equipment levels were deplorable.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told a different session of parliament on Friday that the farm sector would receive 6.1 trillion roubles ($1.07 billion) in budget funds for the first half of this year, when spring sowing takes place.
Russia produced a net 69.3 million tonnes of grain in 1996, after 63.4 million in 1995. Both harvests are among the worst in three decades.

The Duma resolution comes after a Kremlin cabinet re-shuffle that removed Alexander Zaveryukha as deputy prime minister in charge of agriculture, so depriving the reform-wary farm lobby of its main supporter in the government.

Boris Nemtsov, the 37-year-old former governor of Nizhny Novogorod who was appointed first deputy prime minister, is a leading proponent of market-economy reforms and a potential presidential candidate for the year 2000.
